claims.text: Superconductivity in fully solid-solution high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by local chemical disorder.
Local chemical disorder creates spatial variations in electron-phonon coupling strength.
The local cocktail effect enhances superconducting behavior relative to a structurally homogenized state.
The proposed starting alloy is a fully randomized solid solution containing at least five elements at 5 atomic percent or more each.
The starting alloy has substantial local chemical variation.
Controlled annealing can homogenize the microstructure without inducing phase separation.
Annealing can reduce local atomic-scale compositional fluctuations while preserving an overall single-phase solid solution.
Local chemical disorder produces associated micro-strain fields.
Local chemical disorder and associated micro-strain fields modulate the electron-phonon interaction.
As-cast chemical disorder produces local regions with enhanced electron-phonon coupling.
Local enhancement of electron-phonon coupling raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Annealing reduces the spatial variability of electron-phonon coupling.
Reduced electron-phonon coupling variability after annealing causes a lower superconducting transition temperature than in the as-cast baseline.
As-cast, chemically disordered samples will have a higher Tc than annealed, homogenized samples.
As-cast, chemically disordered samples will exhibit stronger superconducting signatures than annealed, homogenized samples.
The proposed mechanism applies only to fully single-phase, disordered high-entropy alloys.
Phase separation, ordering, or precipitate formation may allow factors other than local chemical disorder to dominate superconducting behavior.
